2|ARCHES: A Randomized, Phase III Study of
3|Androgen Deprivation Therapy With
4|Enzalutamide or Placebo in Men With Metastatic
5|Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer
6|Andrew J. Armstrong, MD, ScM1; Russell Z. Szmulewitz, MD2; Daniel P. Petrylak, MD3; Jeffrey Holzbeierlein, MD4; Arnauld Villers, MD5;
7|Arun Azad, MBBS, PhD6; Antonio Alcaraz, MD, PhD7; Boris Alekseev, MD8; Taro Iguchi, MD, PhD9; Neal D. Shore, MD10;
8|Brad Rosbrook, MS11; Jennifer Sugg, MS12; Benoit Baron, MS13; Lucy Chen, MD12; and Arnulf Stenzl, MD14
9|abstract
10|PURPOSE Enzalutamide, a potent androgen-receptor inhibitor, has demonstrated significant benefits in met-
11|astatic and nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of
12|enzalutamide in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC).
13|METHODS ARCHES (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02677896) is a multinational, double-blind, phase III trial,
14|wherein 1,150 men with mHSPC were randomly assigned 1:1 to enzalutamide (160 mg/day) or placebo, plus
15|androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), stratified by disease volume and prior docetaxel chemotherapy. The
16|primary end point was radiographic progression-free survival.
17|RESULTS As of October 14, 2018, the risk of radiographic progression or death was significantly reduced with
18|enzalutamide plus ADT versus placebo plus ADT (hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; median
19|not reached v 19.0 months). Similar significant improvements in radiographic progression-free survival were
20|reported in prespecified subgroups on the basis of disease volume and prior docetaxel therapy. Enzalutamide
21|plus ADT significantly reduced the risk of prostate-specific antigen progression, initiation of new antineoplastic
22|therapy, first symptomatic skeletal event, castration resistance, and reduced risk of pain progression. More men
23|achieved an undetectable prostate-specific antigen level and/or an objective response with enzalutamide plus
24|ADT (P , .001). Patients in both treatment groups reported a high baseline level of quality of life, which was
25|maintained over time. Grade 3 or greater adverse events were reported in 24.3% of patients who received
26|enzalutamide plus ADT versus 25.6% of patients who received placebo plus ADT, with no unexpected adverse
27|events.
28|CONCLUSION Enzalutamide with ADT significantly reduced the risk of metastatic progression or death over time
29|versus placebo plus ADT in men with mHSPC, including those with low-volume disease and/or prior docetaxel,
30|with a safety analysis that seems consistent with the safety profile of enzalutamide in previous clinical trials in
31|castration-resistant prostate cancer.
32|J Clin Oncol 37:2974-2986. © 2019 by American Society of Clinical Oncology
33|Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives 4.0 License
34|INTRODUCTION
35|Globally, prostate cancer was the most common
36|cancer for men, with 1.4 million patients in 2016;
37|mortality was 381,000.1 In the United States, 174,650
38|new cases of prostate cancer are expected in 2019,
39|with 31,620 anticipated deaths.2 The majority of
40|deaths from prostate cancer are due to metastatic
41|disease, identified either at diagnosis or after relapse
42|following local therapies.3
43|Metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC),
44|defined as patients with metastatic disease who have
45|not yet received, or are continuing to respond to,
46|hormone therapy, accounts for up to 5% of annual
47|prostate cancer incidence in the United States.4 An-
48|drogen deprivation therapy (ADT) with a luteinizing
49|hormone-releasing hormone agonist/receptor antag-
50|onist or bilateral orchiectomy has been the standard of
51|care (SOC) for men with mHSPC.5 However, the
52|majority of men with mHSPC who receive ADT alone
53|progress to castration-resistant disease within 1 to
54|3 years, despite experiencing an initial response.5-7
55|Previous trials in men with mHSPC combining ADT with
56|other treatments such as docetaxel chemotherapy6,8
57|or the selective androgen biosynthesis inhibitor abir-
58|aterone acetate,9-11 hereafter referred to as abiraterone,

1|have demonstrated significant clinical benefits, including
2|significantly improved overall survival (OS), and these
3|combinations are now included in treatment guidelines as
4|part of the SOC.12,13 Abiraterone plus ADT is approved in
5|combination with prednisone for men with metastatic
6|high-risk castration-sensitive prostate cancer,14,15 on the
7|basis of the LATITUDE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier:
8|NCT01715285),10 which exclusively enrolled men with
9|high-risk mHSPC and excluded previous chemotherapy.
10|The efficacy and safety of enzalutamide, a potent
11|androgen-receptor (AR) inhibitor,16 has been demon-
12|strated across the spectrum of castration-resistant
13|prostate cancer (CRPC) by numerous, large-scale,
14|randomized, controlled clinical trials.17-21 In addition,
15|a phase II, open-label, single-arm study investigating
16|enzalutamide monotherapy in patients with hormone-
17|na ̈ıve
18|prostate
19|cancer
20|demonstrated
21|long-term
22|re-
23|ductions in prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, with
24|minimal changes in overall bone mineral density and
25|global health status.22-24
26|Two recent studies that investigated abiraterone in addition
27|to ADT excluded men with prior docetaxel chemotherapy
28|and did not include prospective evaluation of results by
29|disease volume (high v low).10,11 ARCHES (Clinical-
30|Trials.gov identifier: NCT02677896) aimed to assess
31|efficacy and safety of enzalutamide plus ADT in men with
32|mHSPC, regardless of prior docetaxel or disease volume.
33|We hypothesized that enzalutamide, in combination with
34|ADT, would prolong radiographic progression-free sur-
35|vival (rPFS) in men with mHSPC, compared with
36|ADT alone.
37|METHODS
38|Study Design and Conduct
39|ARCHES is a multinational, double-blind, randomized,
40|placebo-controlled, phase III trial. The study protocol was
41|approved by local independent review boards and con-
42|ducted according to provisions of the Declaration of
43|Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the
44|International Conference on Harmonisation. All patients
45|provided written informed consent. An independent Data
46|Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) evaluated unblinded
47|safety data on an ongoing basis. Please refer to the Dis-
48|closures for full information on data sharing.
49|Patients and Treatments
50|Eligible patients were adult (defined according to local
51|regulation) males with pathologically confirmed prostate
52|adenocarcinoma, without neuroendocrine differentiation,
53|signet-cell, or small-cell features, and an Eastern Co-
54|operative Oncology Group performance status score of 0 or
55|1. Eligible patients had hormone-sensitive metastatic dis-
56|ease, either de novo or after recurrence after prior local
57|therapy, documented by a positive bone scan, or metastatic
58|lesions on computed tomography or magnetic resonance
59|imaging. Enrollment was based on investigator-assessed
60|metastases; after study entry, metastasis was evaluated by
61|independent central review. Prior ADT and up to six cycles
62|of prior docetaxel chemotherapy were permitted. Patients
63|who experienced disease progression prior to randomiza-
64|tion while receiving ADT and/or docetaxel were excluded.
65|Additional details regarding inclusion/exclusion criteria are
66|provided in the Data Supplement.
67|Patients were centrally randomized 1:1 to enzalutamide
68|(160 mg/day) plus ADT or placebo plus ADT, stratified by
69|disease volume (low v high) and prior docetaxel chemo-
70|therapy for prostate cancer (no cycles, one to five cycles, or
71|six cycles). High-volume disease was defined as presence
72|of metastases involving the viscera, or in the absence of
73|visceral lesions, four or more bone lesions, one or more of
74|which must have been in a bony structure beyond the
75|vertebral column and pelvic bone, per CHAARTED (Clin-
76|icalTrials.gov identifier: NCT00309985) criteria.6 Treat-
77|ment continued until occurrence of unacceptable toxicity,
78|radiographic progression (confirmed by independent cen-
79|tral review), or initiation of an investigational agent or
80|new prostate cancer therapy. Subsequent therapy after
81|treatment discontinuation was permitted per local practice.
82|On the basis of the primary analysis results and DSMB
83|recommendation of study continuation, eligible patients
84|were offered the opportunity to transition to an open-label
85|extension.
86|End Points
87|The primary end point was rPFS, defined as the time from
88|randomization to the first objective evidence of radiographic
89|disease progression, as assessed by independent central
90|review or death (defined as death from any cause within
91|24 weeks from study drug discontinuation), whichever
92|occurred first. The cutoff of 24 weeks from study drug
93|discontinuation (ie, the second long-term follow-up visit) for
94|deaths (in the absence of disease progression) ensured
95|a similar follow-up period as for monitoring of radiographic
96|progression (ie, two 12-week radiologic assessment cycles
97|post-treatment discontinuation). In addition, sensitivity
98|analyses for rPFS were performed, including all deaths (in
99|the absence of evidence of radiographic progression) re-
100|gardless of timing, and radiographic progression docu-
101|mented by central review according to Prostate Cancer
102|Working Group 2 criteria,25 to assess the robustness of the
103|primary analysis; additional details are provided in Data
104|Supplement Table A1. Key secondary end points were time
105|to PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
106|therapy (including cytotoxic and hormone therapies), PSA
107|undetectable rate, objective response rate, time to de-
108|terioration in urinary symptoms, and OS. Other secondary
109|end points included time to first symptomatic skeletal
110|event, time to castration resistance, patient-reported out-
111|comes (PROs), time to deterioration of quality of life (QoL),
112|and time to pain progression. Additional prespecified an-
113|alyses, per a separate PRO statistical analysis plan (SAP),

1|included QoL over time and sensitivity analyses of time
2|to pain progression (using other clinically meaningful
3|threshold criteria). Safety was also assessed. End point
4|definitions are provided in Data Supplement Table A1.
5|Assessments
6|Efficacy assessments included sequential radiographic
7|imaging performed at screening, at week 13, and every
8|subsequent 12 weeks. Radiographic progression events
9|were confirmed by independent central review; details
10|regarding the definition of radiographic progression, in-
11|cluding confirmatory scans required for new bone lesions
12|observed over time, are provided in Data Supplement
13|Table A2. PSA levels were measured at screening, at weeks
14|1, 5, and 13, every subsequent 12 weeks, and 30 days after
15|the last dose or prior to initiation of new antineoplastic
16|therapy for prostate cancer, whichever occurred first. PRO
17|assessments, such as Functional Assessment of Cancer
18|Therapy-Prostate,26 Quality of Life Prostate-Specific
19|questionnaire 25,27 and Brief Pain Inventory-Short
20|Form (BPI-SF), were completed at baseline, week 13,
21|and every 12 weeks thereafter. Adverse events (AEs) were
22|graded by the investigator according to the National
23|Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Ad-
24|verse Events (version 4.03).
25|Statistical Analysis
26|The final rPFS analysis was planned to occur after
27|262 events, to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.67 with 90%
28|power, on the basis of a two-sided log-rank test and 5%
29|significance level. To adjust for multiplicity, a parallel testing
30|strategy was applied to the key secondary end points
31|(Appendix Fig A1, online only). Key secondary end
32|points, other than OS, were sequentially tested at a 1%
33|significance level. A final OS analysis will be performed
34|when 342 deaths have occurred to provide 80% power to
35|detect an HR of 0.73 at a 4% significance level. An interim
36|OS analysis was performed at the time of the final rPFS
37|analysis at a significance level calculated using the O'Brien-
38|Fleming function to control the overall alpha. Additional
39|details regarding the statistical analyses (original and final)
40|are provided in the Data Supplement (Fig A1 and Table A1)
41|and Protocol (including SAP).
42|RESULTS
43|Patients and Treatment
44|From March 21, 2016, to January 12, 2018, a total of 1,150
45|patients were randomly assigned 1:1 from 202 centers in
46|North and Latin America, Europe, and Asia; 1,146 patients
47|received at least one dose of the study drug (Fig 1).
48|Baseline demographics were well balanced between
49|treatment groups (Table 1); 727 patients (63.2%) had high-
50|volume disease, and 205 (17.9%) received prior docetaxel
51|chemotherapy. Use of concomitant antiandrogens as
52|prostate cancer therapy during the study was reported by
53|34 patients (5.9%) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group and
54|43 patients (7.5%) in the placebo plus ADT group.
55|As of the data cutoff on October 14, 2018, median follow-up
56|time was 14.4 months. Overall, 377 patients (32.8%) dis-
57|continued study treatment (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 135
58|[23.5%]; placebo plus ADT, n = 242 [42.0%]). The primary
59|reason for treatment discontinuation was progressive dis-
60|ease (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 65 [11.3%] v placebo plus
61|ADT, n = 171 [29.7%]), followed by patient withdrawal
62|(n = 25 [4.4%] v n = 30 [5.2%], respectively; Fig 1).
63|rPFS
64|At data cutoff, 292 radiographic disease progression events
65|or deaths without radiographic disease progression within
66|24 weeks of treatment discontinuation had occurred
67|(enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 91 [15.9%]; placebo plus
68|ADT, n = 201 [34.9%]; Table 2). Overall, enzalutamide plus
69|ADT significantly reduced the risk of radiographic disease
70|progression or death compared with placebo plus ADT by
71|61% (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.30 to 0.50; P , .001; Fig 2A).
72|Median rPFS was not reached (NR) with enzalutamide plus
73|ADT (95% CI, NR to NR) versus 19.0 months (95% CI, 16.6
74|to 22.2 months) with placebo plus ADT. The treatment
75|effect of enzalutamide plus ADT was consistent across all
76|prespecified subgroups, including disease volume and
77|prior docetaxel chemotherapy (Fig 2B). A sensitivity
78|analysis of rPFS, including all deaths (in the absence of
79|evidence of radiographic disease progression) regardless of
80|timing, and a sensitivity analysis of radiographic progres-
81|sion documented by central review according to Prostate
82|Cancer Working Group 2 criteria25 were both consistent
83|with the primary analysis (Table 2).
84|Secondary End Points
85|The superiority of enzalutamide plus ADT over placebo plus
86|ADT was shown for the key secondary end points of time to
87|PSA progression, time to initiation of new antineoplastic
88|therapy, PSA undetectable rate, and objective response
89|rate (Table 2; Fig 3). Although the median time to initiation
90|of a new antineoplastic agent of 30.2 months in the
91|enzalutamide arm is not a reliable estimate because it
92|resulted from an event observed in the only remaining
93|patient at risk, the treatment effect was robust, as evi-
94|denced by the HR of 0.28 (95% CI, 0.20 to 0.40; P , .001).
95|Of the patients who initiated new antineoplastic therapy, the
96|most common therapy was abiraterone (n = 13; 28.3%)
97|followed by docetaxel (n = 11; 23.9%) in the enzalutamide
98|plus ADT group and docetaxel (n = 52; 39.1%) followed by
99|abiraterone and enzalutamide (n = 28 each; 21.1%) in the
100|placebo plus ADT group (Data Supplement Table A3). At
101|this interim OS analysis, data were immature, with
102|84 deaths (enzalutamide plus ADT, n = 39; placebo plus ADT,
103|n = 45); median duration of OS was NR in either treatment
104|group (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.25; P = .3361; Table 2;
105|Data Supplement Fig A2). Enzalutamide plus ADT also
106|significantly reduced the risk of a first symptomatic skeletal

2|Data Supplement Fig A3).
3|Mean Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Prostate
4|total score, as a global indicator of QoL, was high at baseline
5|for both treatment groups (Table 1) and remained high over
6|time (Data Supplement Fig A4). Enzalutamide plus ADT did
7|not significantly affect time to deterioration in urinary
8|symptoms or QoL compared with placebo plus ADT
9|(Table 2). Although the analysis of time to pain progression,
10|with progression defined as a 30% or greater increase from
11|baseline in average BPI-SF pain severity score, was not
12|delayed (Table 2), prespecified sensitivity analyses from the
13|PRO SAP, using a clinically significant 2-point or greater
14|increase from baseline in average BPI-SF score as the
15|progression threshold, demonstrated that enzalutamide
16|plus ADT delayed time to pain progression for worst pain
17|and pain severity versus placebo plus ADT (Table 2; Data
18|Supplement Fig A5).
19|Safety
20|Median treatment duration was 12.8 months (range,
21|0.2 to 26.6 months) in the enzalutamide plus ADT group
22|and 11.6 months (range, 0.2 to 24.6 months) in the
23|placebo plus ADT group. Grade 3 or greater AEs, serious
24|AEs, and AEs leading to treatment discontinuation were
25|reported in similar proportions of patients in both treat-
26|ment groups (Table 3). There were no unexpected AEs; of
27|the 14 AEs (2.4%) leading to death in the enzalutamide
28|plus ADT group and 10 (1.7%) in the placebo plus ADT
29|group, none were assessed by the investigator to be re-
30|lated to treatment in the enzalutamide plus ADT group,
